newsitem.title: GERMANY: German industry lobby attacks Bonn tax reforms.
newsitem.headline: German industry lobby attacks Bonn tax reforms.

text.p: Germany's leading industrial lobby group attacked government tax reforms passed by the lower house of parliament on Thursday, saying they had been amended to raise, instead of cut, the tax burden on businesses.
The Federation of German Industry (BDI) said that, in its current form, Finance Minister Theo Waigel's two-year package of tax reforms was no longer acceptable.
"Instead of bringing vital relief to industry, the tax burden will in future rise," the BDI said in a statement.

BDI head Hans-Olaf Henkel last week slammed as a "scandal" changes to the reforms which would limit tax writeoffs against company losses and end tax relief on reserves built up by power generators to pay to decommission nuclear plants.

"The latest decision to limit writing off tax against losses will make it difficult, if not impossible, for companies to carry out crisis management," the statement continued. "This must have a negative impact on investment."
The Bundestag lower house passed Waigel's 1998 and 1999 tax bills, which would cut corporate tax rates while scrapping a range of tax exemptions.

The measures now go to the Bundesrat upper house, which is controlled by the opposition Social Democrats, where they face certain defeat on July 4. Rejection in the Bundesrat will force parliament's mediation process to be invoked.
"If no solutions are found in mediation to improve the investment climate in Germany, the government's original goal of halving unemployment will recede into the distant future," the BDI said.
